classification.difficultyReason: List consecutive integers satisfying two strict bounds.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply strict bounds to negative integers; part c applies the same method across zero. Comparing and ordering integers is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines integer order on a number line. Example 1 lists consecutive integers strictly between two bounds, excluding both endpoints.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List consecutive integers satisfying two strict bounds.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct equally spaced number lines and locate signed integers; part c also requires excluding both stated bounds before plotting the intervening integers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b require locating specified integers on a student-drawn line. Part c additionally selects integers satisfying strict inequalities before plotting them.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 explains equally spaced integers, negatives left of zero and positives right of zero. Example 2 marks every integer strictly between two bounds with dots. Page 3 Example 3 reinforces plotting integer points.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Draw equally spaced number lines and mark specified integers or integers satisfying strict bounds.

classification.difficultyReason: The step is explicitly supplied: add three successively to the last term to obtain the next three negative integers.

questions.mappingNote: The stated increase of three is applied successively to the last given term, using the same repeated-step method.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 continues integer sequences by repeated equal steps; part b demonstrates increasing a negative sequence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Continue an integer sequence using the explicitly supplied increment of three.

classification.difficultyReason: Continue an integer sequence by repeatedly subtracting the stated positive step.

questions.mappingNote: This question applies the same decreasing-sequence method, subtracting four successively.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 continues integer sequences by their stated constant step, including through zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Continue an integer sequence by repeatedly subtracting the stated positive step.

classification.difficultyReason: Continue an integer sequence using the explicitly supplied increment of seven.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 applies the same increasing-sequence method with an increment of seven.
questions.methodNote: Example 3 continues integer sequences by repeatedly adding or subtracting the stated positive increment, illustrated on number lines.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Continue an integer sequence using the explicitly supplied increment of seven.

classification.difficultyReason: Read four temperatures directly from uniformly subdivided Celsius scales.

questions.mappingNote: Each response interprets an integer Celsius reading from a subdivided vertical scale; interpreting integers in context is the primary assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 1 interprets negative temperatures as below zero; page 2 explains equally spaced integer scales and their order. Page 3 was inspected but its sequence and opposite-number methods are not required here.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read four temperatures directly from uniformly subdivided Celsius scales.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught opposite-integer rule by reversing each sign while retaining its magnitude.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the source definition of opposite integers. The closest supplied skill is locating integers on a number line.
questions.methodNote: Take the matching integer the same distance from zero on the other side, as taught under ‘The opposite of an integer’.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the integer equally far from zero on the opposite side.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct addition of a positive integer to a negative integer using the method in Example 4.

questions.mappingNote: Every part adds a positive integer to a negative integer, directly matching Example 4 and add-subtract-positive-integers. No subtraction of negative integers is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Page 4 introduces signed quantities in context. Page 5 teaches addition of a positive integer by moving right on the number line; Example 4 applies this to negative starting values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct addition of a positive integer to a negative integer using the method in Example 4.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct subtraction of a positive integer, including crossing zero.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses subtraction of a positive integer; no touching-sign rewrite or additional operation is required.
questions.methodNote: Subtract a positive integer by moving left along the number line. Page 5 explains this and Example 5 demonstrates subtraction from positive and negative starting values.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct subtraction of a positive integer, including crossing zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct addition and subtraction of positive integers, including crossing zero.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly applies the movement method to addition or subtraction of a positive integer; larger values retain the same method.
questions.methodNote: Addition of a positive integer moves right along the number line; subtraction of a positive integer moves left. Page 5 Examples 4 and 5 demonstrate these methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct addition and subtraction of positive integers, including crossing zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive additions or subtractions of positive integers, working from left to right through negative values.

questions.mappingNote: Each part combines the positive-integer additions and subtractions demonstrated on page 5. The explicit question instruction supplies the left-to-right sequence.
questions.methodNote: Adding a positive integer moves right on the number line; subtracting a positive integer moves left. Apply these operations successively from left to right.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive additions or subtractions of positive integers, working from left to right through negative values.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the signs of two addends to add magnitudes or find their difference and assign the result's sign, including sums that cross zero.

questions.mappingNote: Parts b, c, e, j and l use the rightward movement demonstrated in page 5 Example 4. Parts a, d, f, g, h, i and k use page 7 Example 6 and the two-line rewrite demonstrated in page 8 Example 7a–b. The source margin explicitly refers to Examples 6, 7a, b.
questions.methodNote: Adding a positive integer moves right on a number line. Adding a negative integer subtracts its opposite; rewrite the operation and evaluate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate single additions of positive and negative integers, including crossing zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish subtraction of positive and negative integers, replace subtraction of a negative with addition, and evaluate the resulting signed calculation.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b, c, e and i use page 5's positive-integer subtraction method. Parts d, f, g, h, j, k and l use page 8's rule and Examples 7c–e and 8. The printed example reference is retained in the prompt.
questions.methodNote: Subtract a positive integer by moving left on a number line. Subtract a negative integer by adding its opposite, then evaluate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate single subtractions of positive or negative integers using the taught sign rule.

classification.difficultyReason: Single-operation integer calculations using the taught rules for adding and subtracting negative integers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e apply the addition rule on page 7 and Example 7(a–b) on page 8. Parts f–h apply the subtraction rule and Example 7(c–e) on page 8. Part i applies subtraction of a positive integer as demonstrated on page 5.
questions.methodNote: Adding a negative integer means subtracting its opposite; subtracting a negative integer means adding its opposite. Subtracting a positive integer moves left on the number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Single-operation integer calculations using the taught rules for adding and subtracting negative integers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-term directed-number expressions, including adding and subtracting negative integers.

questions.mappingNote: Question 4 is explicitly linked to Example 9 on PDF page 9. Parts a, d, f, h, i, j, k and l require rewriting negative operands; b, c, e and g apply directed addition and subtraction directly.
questions.methodNote: Adding a negative integer subtracts its opposite; subtracting a negative integer adds its opposite. Rewrite touching signs, then evaluate addition and subtraction from left to right, as in Example 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-term directed-number expressions, including adding and subtracting negative integers.

classification.difficultyReason: Rewrite subtraction of a negative as addition, then compare magnitudes to determine the sign of each difference; larger numbers add arithmetic rather than new reasoning.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 explicitly references Example 11. Part a follows Example 11b; parts b and d follow Example 11d; part c follows Example 11c after rewriting subtraction of a negative.
questions.methodNote: Subtract a negative integer by adding its opposite. Example 11 evaluates larger directed numbers by rewriting touching signs, then calculating the difference of magnitudes with the appropriate sign.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the subtraction-of-a-negative rule and calculate with larger integers.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the rise as maximum minus minimum and calculate the positive difference between two negative temperatures using the taught method.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 Example 10 directly models the difference between a negative maximum and a negative minimum temperature; page 8 supplies the subtraction rule.
questions.methodNote: Calculate maximum temperature minus minimum temperature, rewriting subtraction of a negative as addition of its opposite.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a temperature rise by subtracting a negative minimum from a negative maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate the temperature change into final minus initial, subtract a negative, and describe the positive result as an increase.

questions.mappingNote: Question 7 applies the same method to a rise from −2°C to 9°C: 9 − (−2) = 11.
questions.methodNote: Example 10 calculates temperature difference by subtracting the minimum temperature from the maximum and rewriting subtraction of a negative as addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a temperature increase across zero by subtracting the initial negative temperature.

classification.difficultyReason: Read each minimum–maximum pair and calculate maximum minus minimum, handling both negative maxima and changes across zero; the table repeats the same method.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 Example 10 directly demonstrates the temperature-difference calculation; page 8 supplies the subtraction-of-a-negative rule used in every row.
questions.methodNote: Calculate maximum minus minimum; subtracting a negative integer means adding its opposite.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate seven temperature increases by subtracting a negative minimum from the maximum.

classification.difficultyReason: Model a temperature change by subtracting the initial temperature from the final temperature.

questions.mappingNote: Page 9 Example 10 models a temperature difference using subtraction. Page 5 supplies the subtraction-of-a-positive-integer method needed for −2 − 8.
questions.methodNote: Subtract the initial temperature from the final temperature; subtracting a positive integer moves left on the number line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model a temperature change by subtracting the initial temperature from the final temperature.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the product sign from whether the two factors have matching signs, then multiply their magnitudes directly.

questions.mappingNote: Every part a–p assesses direct multiplication of signed integers. Parts k, m and n use the two-negative rule; all other parts use the different-sign rule. The printed margin reference is Example 12.
questions.methodNote: Multiply the magnitudes and apply the product sign rule: different signs give a negative product; two negative factors give a positive product. Example 12 demonstrates direct signed products and rewrites two negative factors as a positive multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct multiplication of two integers using the taught sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the matching-sign or different-sign quotient rule and divide the magnitudes; every part uses the same direct procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses direct signed integer division. Parts a–e and o–p use a negative dividend and positive divisor; f–j use a positive dividend and negative divisor; k–n use two negative operands. The page 12 quotient rules and page 13 Example 13 directly support these cases.
questions.methodNote: Divide the magnitudes and apply the quotient sign rule: different signs give a negative quotient; two negative operands give a positive quotient. Example 13 shows direct one-line signed division.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct integer divisions using the quotient sign rules demonstrated in Example 13.

classification.difficultyReason: Read the fraction bar as division and apply the taught quotient sign rule to small integer magnitudes.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly assesses signed integer division in fraction notation.
questions.methodNote: The quotient sign rules on page 12 and Example 14 on page 13 treat the fraction bar as division: different signs give a negative quotient and two negative signs give a positive quotient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate single integer quotients written as fractions.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate integer quotients with larger magnitudes and mixed signs.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts require signed integer division; the larger magnitudes do not change the assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Use the quotient sign rules on page 12 and the fraction notation demonstrated in Example 14 on page 13, dividing magnitudes and applying the sign.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate integer quotients with larger magnitudes and mixed signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive signed products and quotients, working from left to right.

questions.mappingNote: Each expression has two multiplication or division operations, so order of operations with integers is the closest most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply the product sign rules and Example 12 to each multiplication, and the quotient rules and Example 13 to division. Successive operations of equal precedence are evaluated from left to right.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive signed products and quotients, working from left to right.

classification.difficultyReason: Recover missing signed factors and divisors using inverse multiplication and division.

questions.mappingNote: The response is an unknown factor or divisor rather than a quotient alone; inverse operations is the closest assessed skill. The supplied fraction and negative-index reuse candidates have different complete tasks and are not reused.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 explicitly links multiplication and equivalent division statements. Use that inverse relationship with the integer sign rules to recover a factor or divisor, then check by substitution.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover missing signed factors and divisors using inverse multiplication and division.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish a bracketed negative base from an external minus, evaluate powers first, and combine the resulting signed factors, especially in part e.

questions.mappingNote: Page 14 explicitly contrasts negative bases with external negatives. Page 15 Example 15 a and b supplies the repeated-factor method for a, b and f–k; its order-of-operations rule and Example 16 e support evaluating powers before the multiplications in c–e.
questions.methodNote: Expand a power as repeated multiplication. A negative base in brackets is repeatedly multiplied; an external minus is applied after the power. Evaluate powers before multiplication.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate integer powers and apply powers before external negatives and multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two successive additions or subtractions while retaining intermediate signs and rewriting subtraction of a negative where needed.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts assess sequential integer addition and subtraction within Exercise 4E's order-of-operations context. Parts b, d and f additionally require the subtraction-of-a-negative rule.
questions.methodNote: Carry out addition and subtraction from left to right, as demonstrated in Example 15c. To subtract a negative integer, add its opposite, as demonstrated on page 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate three-term integer expressions from left to right, rewriting subtraction of a negative where necessary.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate bracket evaluation, signed multiplication, and the final addition or subtraction; part h also requires converting subtraction of a negative after multiplication.

questions.mappingNote: Example 16a directly supports a and d; Example 16b supports b, e, f, g and h through evaluating brackets before multiplication and the final addition or subtraction. Example 15c supports c through left-to-right addition and subtraction. The order-of-operations rule on page 15 applies to every part.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Adding a negative is subtraction of its opposite. Page 15 Example 16 demonstrates bracket substitution and successive integer calculations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply brackets first, multiplication next, and addition and subtraction from left to right to integer expressions.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply operation precedence while distinguishing an external negative from subtraction and selecting the correct sign for products involving negative bracket results.

questions.mappingNote: Page 15, Examples 15 and 16, directly models the operation order used throughout a–i. Pages 5 and 7 support the bracket differences and additions in a–e; page 11 supports the product signs in e–i. The leading negative in a and b takes the opposite of the bracket result.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Adding a negative subtracts its opposite. Two negative factors give a positive product; factors of different signs give a negative product.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate brackets before multiplication and addition or subtraction, applying integer sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed integer expressions before multiplication and addition or subtraction, including subtraction of a negative integer.

questions.mappingNote: Page 15 states the order of operations; Example 16a–c directly models the bracketed products and differences in a–f, and the same sequence applies to g–h. Page 7 supports rewriting addition of a negative in g; page 5 supports directed addition and subtraction. These expressions directly assess integer order of operations.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then multiplication, then addition and subtraction. Retain signed intermediate values and simplify one stage per line.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed integer expressions before multiplication and addition or subtraction, including subtraction of a negative integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two multiplication or division operations from left to right, applying integer sign rules.

questions.mappingNote: Page 15 explicitly gives the left-to-right rule for multiplication and division. Page 12 provides integer product examples and quotient sign rules, directly supporting all four calculations.
questions.methodNote: Perform multiplication and division from left to right. Different signs give a negative product or quotient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two multiplication or division operations from left to right, applying integer sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine powers of negative integers with multiplication and addition, applying the operation order and sign rules.

questions.mappingNote: Page 14 distinguishes powers of negative bases from external negative signs. Page 15 gives the operation order, demonstrates negative squares in Example 15 and combines powers, products and addition in Example 16(e), directly supporting all four parts.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate powers first, then multiplication from left to right, then addition. A parenthesised negative base has a positive square and a negative cube.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine powers of negative integers with multiplication and addition, applying the operation order and sign rules.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate a total cost, then subtract it from sales revenue to obtain a negative financial result.

questions.mappingNote: Page 15 teaches multiplication before addition and subtraction; page 5 connects negative financial amounts with debt. This question applies those methods to purchase cost and sales revenue.
questions.methodNote: Calculate multiplication before subtraction. Subtracting a larger positive amount produces a negative result, interpreted as a debt or loss.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate a total cost, then subtract it from sales revenue to obtain a negative financial result.

classification.difficultyReason: Model repeated deposits by multiplication, carry that balance into the scaffolded second part, and subtract the cheque to interpret a negative bank balance.

questions.mappingNote: Page 5 explains subtraction of a positive integer and interprets a negative result as debt. Page 15 gives the operation sequence and worked integer calculations. These support the multiplication in part a and subtraction past zero in part b.
questions.methodNote: Multiply the monthly deposit by the number of months, then subtract the cheque amount. A negative balance represents debt.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Model repeated deposits by multiplication, then subtract a cheque exceeding the balance.

classification.difficultyReason: Set up coordinate axes on the supplied blank grid and translate each ordered pair into horizontal and vertical movement, including zero coordinates on axes.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess plotting integer-coordinate points, including three points on axes. The supplied reuse candidate assesses reading different plotted points and is not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Read the horizontal coordinate first and the vertical coordinate second. Move right or left from the origin according to the first coordinate, then up or down according to the second. A zero coordinate places the point on an axis.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot given integer coordinates in all four quadrants and on both axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Read integer coordinates, including points on axes, and count points using coordinate signs.

questions.mappingNote: All responses directly assess identifying Cartesian coordinates and interpreting their signs. The offered reuse candidate has different plotted coordinates and lacks part b, so it is not source-equivalent.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 introduces perpendicular coordinate axes and horizontal-first ordered coordinates. Page 18 demonstrates reading labelled points, including points on axes, in Example 17 and explains positive and negative horizontal and vertical directions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read integer coordinates, including points on axes, and count points using coordinate signs.

classification.difficultyReason: Plot and join coordinates, classify the resulting figures, and select area dimensions; the trapezia require recognising parallel sides and their perpendicular separation, while part e requires recognising perpendicular oblique lines.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts require coordinate plotting. Parts a–d and f additionally assess shape classification and area; part e assesses perpendicular lines. These are represented by secondary skills, but their original source-taught prerequisite methods remain unverified.
questions.methodNote: Page 17 introduces perpendicular coordinate axes and ordered horizontal and vertical coordinates. Page 18 demonstrates plotting by horizontal movement followed by vertical movement, including negative coordinates. No supplied teaching page establishes the required area formulas, shape-classification methods or a method for checking the non-axis-aligned perpendicular lines.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct coordinate figures, identify their properties and derive areas or a relationship between lines.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose quarter-unit subdivisions and locate signed mixed numbers between adjacent integers, keeping negative fractional positions in the correct direction.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 establishes equal spacing and plotting; page 3 explains opposite positions about zero; page 20 explicitly plots negative fractions and mixed numbers. The closest catalogue skill covers ordering signed fractional values, with integer number-line placement as supporting knowledge.
questions.methodNote: Use equally spaced number-line ticks. Negative fractions lie left of zero and opposite fractions lie equal distances from zero. Locate fractional positions between adjacent integers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Locate signed mixed numbers using halves and quarters between integer ticks.

classification.difficultyReason: Order signed fractions with unlike denominators, including double-negative fractions and a negative mixed number.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess ordering unlike signed fractions. The supplied Chapter 4 evidence supports signed ordering but does not establish the referenced Chapter 2 comparison method.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 establishes left-to-right number-line ordering. Page 3 explains opposites. Page 20 locates negative fractions and demonstrates equivalent fractions for addition and subtraction, while referring prior fraction teaching to Chapter 2. The authored comparison solutions use exact common-denominator equivalence; the source's prior comparison procedure remains unverified.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Order signed fractions with unlike denominators, including double-negative fractions and a negative mixed number.

classification.difficultyReason: Link mixed-number conversion, common-denominator selection, signed numerator arithmetic, and simplification; part t additionally requires rewriting subtraction of a negative.

questions.mappingNote: Example 18a–b supports integer and mixed-number additions in a, b, i, j, m and n. Example 18c–d directly supports signed fraction calculations in c–h and k–t. Page 21 Example 20b also demonstrates conversion of a negative mixed number to an improper fraction. The primary skill is fraction addition and subtraction; t additionally assesses rewriting subtraction of a negative.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 Example 18 demonstrates signed fraction addition and subtraction, including equivalent fractions with common denominators. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, retain signs, combine numerators over a common denominator, and simplify. Page 3 explains taking the opposite; subtracting a negative in t adds its positive opposite.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add and subtract signed fractions and mixed numbers, including unlike denominators and subtraction of a negative fraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide the magnitudes, express the remainder as the fractional part of an exact mixed number, and apply the quotient sign rule.

questions.mappingNote: All three parts directly apply Example 19's division of signed integers giving fractional quotients. Signed division is the primary assessed skill; expressing the exact quotient as a mixed number is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Example 19 first divides the positive magnitudes, retaining the remainder as a fraction in a mixed number, then assigns a negative sign for different signs or a positive sign for matching signs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide signed integers and express non-integral quotients exactly as mixed numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Determine product signs, multiply fraction factors, and simplify; part e extends the same procedure to three factors without requiring a new strategy.

questions.mappingNote: These examples directly support a–d and f–h. Part e applies the same signed-fraction multiplication successively to three factors. The assessed skill is multiplication of fractions with sign determination.
questions.methodNote: Example 20a multiplies a negative fraction by an integer; Example 20d replaces the product of two negative fractions with the corresponding positive product, then multiplies numerators and denominators. Simplify exact fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Multiply signed fractions and integers, simplify products and evaluate one three-factor product.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the taught reciprocal and sign rules, simplify products, and convert improper fractions where needed; every part uses the same direct procedure.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess signed fraction division. Parts a, b, d, e and g divide by negative fractions; c, f and h divide by positive numbers. Mixed-number answers in b and e follow the teacher key and the conversions illustrated on pages 20–21.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 Example 20 b and c replaces division by multiplication by the reciprocal and simplifies. Example 19 applies the same-sign and different-sign quotient rules; Example 20 d demonstrates two negative factors giving a positive result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide signed fractions by multiplying by reciprocals, then simplify.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine signed fractions and mixed numbers, evaluating brackets and multiplication before addition and subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 14–15 establish order of operations, including bracket-first calculations and multiplication before addition. Page 20 Example 18 demonstrates common-denominator signed fraction arithmetic, supporting a–i. Page 21 Example 20 demonstrates signed fraction multiplication and conversion of a mixed number to an improper fraction, supporting b–e and i. Page 20 explicitly extends the earlier integer arithmetic to fractions; g applies subtraction of a negative.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first and multiplication before addition or subtraction. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions where useful, use common denominators for signed addition and subtraction, and simplify exactly.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine signed fractions and mixed numbers, evaluating brackets and multiplication before addition and subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines signed fraction arithmetic, mixed-number conversion and multiplication or division before addition.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, b and f apply Example 18's common-denominator method. Parts c, d and e combine the signed products or reciprocal division of Examples 19–20 with fraction addition. Multiplication and division of fractions is the most advanced directly assessed catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Example 18 uses common denominators for signed fraction addition and subtraction. Examples 19–20 apply sign rules, convert mixed numbers to improper fractions and replace division by multiplication by the reciprocal. Perform multiplication and division before addition and subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines signed fraction arithmetic, mixed-number conversion and multiplication or division before addition.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of negative fractions, then multiply and simplify where required.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d assess powers of negative fractions directly. Parts e–h additionally require multiplication after evaluating the power. Page 20 explicitly extends integer arithmetic to fractions, while pages 14–15 establish bracketed negative bases and operation order.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate the power of the entire bracketed negative fraction first, then perform multiplication and simplify exactly. Even powers give positive results and odd powers give negative results. Page 15 places powers before multiplication; page 21 Example 20 applies signed multiplication to fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of negative fractions, then multiply and simplify where required.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply signed addition or rewrite subtraction of a negative as addition, then calculate; no operation selection or modelling is needed.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, d, f, g, h, i and k add negative integers using the page 7 rule. Parts b, c, e and j add positive integers by moving right, consistent with the number-line model. Part l uses the page 8 subtraction-of-a-negative rule. The shared task principally assesses integer addition and subtraction.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 explains addition of a negative integer as movement left and subtraction of its opposite. Page 8 explains subtraction of a negative integer as movement right and addition of its opposite; Example 7 demonstrates rewriting touching signs before calculation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate twelve sums and differences of directed integers, including addition and subtraction of negative integers.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate seven wickets into a total penalty using the supplied scoring rule, then combine that negative total with the runs.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is constructing a directed number sentence from the scoring definition, then adding the negative penalty total.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 explains that adding a negative integer is equivalent to subtracting its opposite; page 8 applies this rule in numerical calculations. Seven wicket penalties contribute a total of -35, which is added to the 25 runs.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate runs and wicket penalties into a directed number sentence and evaluate it.

classification.difficultyReason: Match the minimum and maximum temperatures to each explicitly ordered subtraction, then apply subtraction of a negative.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts substitute the given temperatures in the specified order, then rewrite subtraction of a negative as addition of its positive opposite. Integer subtraction is the principal assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 8 states that subtracting a negative number means adding its opposite. Examples 7 and 8 rewrite the subtraction before evaluating; page 7 establishes directed addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute two negative temperatures into ordered differences and subtract negative integers.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute inside and outside temperatures into the supplied subtraction orders and calculate the corresponding positive and negative differences.

questions.mappingNote: Part a substitutes the inside and outside temperatures in that order and rewrites subtraction of −5 as addition of 5. Part b reverses the temperature order and subtracts 22 from −5. Modelling the requested differences is the principal assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Subtracting a negative integer means adding its opposite, as stated on page 8. Number-line explanations on pages 7–8 establish leftward movement for subtraction of a positive integer and addition of a negative integer.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate two specified temperature differences into directed-number subtractions, preserving the requested order.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose the product sign from the two factor signs and multiply their magnitudes; larger numbers add arithmetic work without further reasoning.

questions.mappingNote: All parts a–l directly assess multiplication of integers. Parts a, b, c, e, i, j and l have unlike signs; parts d, f, g, h and k have two negative factors.
questions.methodNote: Use the product sign rules on page 11: unlike signs give a negative product and two negative factors give a positive product. Multiply the magnitudes, following Example 12 on page 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply integer multiplication sign rules to twelve products.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply integer quotient sign rules and divide whole-number magnitudes.

questions.mappingNote: Page 12 explicitly establishes all signed-division cases required by parts a–l. Each part directly assesses multiplication and division of integers.
questions.methodNote: Divide the magnitudes and apply the quotient sign rule: different signs give a negative quotient; two negatives give a positive quotient.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply integer quotient sign rules and divide whole-number magnitudes.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed integer calculations before multiplying, and distinguish a squared negative number from its opposite.

questions.mappingNote: Pages 7–8 support directed addition and subtraction; page 11 supplies signed multiplication. Page 14 explicitly distinguishes a negative square from the square of a negative number. Page 15 gives the order-of-operations rule and Examples 15–16, including bracket-first products and powers. These methods directly cover all nine parts.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then powers, then multiplication. Apply the signed-product rules. In part f, square the parenthesised negative integer before applying the leading minus.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed integer calculations before multiplying, and distinguish a squared negative number from its opposite.

classification.difficultyReason: Set up suitable coordinate axes on the blank grid and translate each ordered pair into horizontal and vertical movement, including zero coordinates.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 defines horizontal and vertical coordinates and unit axes. Page 18 demonstrates locating labelled points by horizontal movement followed by vertical movement, including negative coordinates. This directly supports all six requested plots.
questions.methodNote: Use unit coordinate axes. The first coordinate determines horizontal movement from the origin; the second determines vertical movement. Negative coordinates indicate left or down.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Plot six given integer coordinate pairs, including points on both axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Read seven integer coordinate pairs from a unit Cartesian grid, including points on the axes.

questions.mappingNote: Page 17 defines coordinate order and unit axes. Page 18 demonstrates reading labelled points in all quadrants and on axes in Example 17, directly matching this task.
questions.methodNote: Read the horizontal coordinate first and the vertical coordinate second, using signed unit distances from the origin. A point on an axis has zero for the other coordinate.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Read seven integer coordinate pairs from a unit Cartesian grid, including points on the axes.

classification.difficultyReason: Add and subtract signed fractions and mixed numbers using simple common denominators.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly assess signed fraction addition or subtraction. Parts a, b and f combine a negative fraction or mixed number with a positive integer; c and d have equal denominators; e combines the negative-addition rule with equivalent fractions.
questions.methodNote: Page 20 explicitly extends signed-integer arithmetic to fractions. Example 18 evaluates negative fractions and negative mixed numbers, uses common denominators and simplifies results. Pages 7–8 establish rewriting addition of a negative as subtraction and subtraction of a negative as addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Add and subtract signed fractions and mixed numbers using simple common denominators.

classification.difficultyReason: Combines signed fraction products and quotients, mixed-number conversion and multiplication or division before subtraction.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–e, g and h directly assess signed fraction multiplication or division; b also converts a mixed number. Parts f and i combine fraction operations using precedence and common denominators. The closest primary catalogue skill is multiply-divide-fractions.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 Example 20 converts mixed numbers to improper fractions, replaces division by multiplication by the reciprocal, and applies sign rules to fraction products. Page 20 Example 18 uses common denominators for fraction subtraction. Page 14 demonstrates multiplication before addition and the effect of brackets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combines signed fraction products and quotients, mixed-number conversion and multiplication or division before subtraction.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate positive and negative voltage extremes using decimal factors, then find their difference.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed calculation uses signed decimal multiples of 230 and subtraction of the negative minimum. Decimal multiplication is the closest primary skill; contextual modelling and integer subtraction support the final difference.
questions.methodNote: Page 11 establishes that a negative factor times a positive factor gives a negative product. Page 8 teaches subtracting a negative by adding its opposite. Original teaching evidence for multiplying decimals by whole numbers was not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate positive and negative voltage extremes using decimal factors, then find their difference.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate the powers using negative-factor multiplication, then identify and state the even–odd pattern supported by the five calculated results.

questions.mappingNote: All five calculations and the concluding observation assess the effect of index parity on powers of a negative base; sign-of-powers is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 14 distinguishes a power of a bracketed negative number from a leading negative sign. Page 15 Example 15 expands a bracketed negative square into repeated multiplication. The solutions extend repeated multiplication by pairing negative factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate powers of negative one and describe the alternating results using odd and even indices.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret successive positions and turns, calculate four positive travel distances and distinguish total distance from displacement.

questions.mappingNote: The task models a contextual journey through directed positions; total distance requires adding all four walking legs, including the return to A.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 establishes equally spaced integer positions and left/right order. Page 5 models movement right for addition and left for subtraction. Count the distance between each successive pair of positions and add the positive distances.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret successive positions and turns, calculate four positive travel distances and distinguish total distance from displacement.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate means of signed integer lists by summing and dividing, including a fractional result.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies this embedded averaging method to a signed integer list; the primary skill assesses calculating a mean.
questions.methodNote: Question 17 explicitly defines the average as the sum divided by the number of values and supplies equivalent division and fraction demonstrations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate means of signed integer lists by summing and dividing, including a fractional result.

classification.difficultyReason: Calculate means of signed fractions and mixed numbers using common denominators and division by the number of values.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly assesses calculating a mean; fraction addition and division support that calculation.
questions.methodNote: Question 17 defines the average as the sum divided by the number of values and demonstrates both division notation and a fraction with the sum as numerator. Question 18 applies that same method to signed fractions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Calculate means of signed fractions and mixed numbers using common denominators and division by the number of values.

classification.difficultyReason: Substitute signed mixed numbers into eight expressions, including products and grouped fraction numerators.

questions.mappingNote: The most advanced directly assessed skill is substitution of negative values into expressions. The supplied chapter evidence supports the subsequent signed fraction calculations, but does not establish prerequisite substitution notation, juxtaposed multiplication or fraction-bar grouping. Method review remains unresolved until original prerequisite teaching is supplied.
questions.methodNote: Pages 11–12 teach signs of products and quotients; pages 14–15 teach grouping and operation order; pages 20–21 extend signed arithmetic to fractions, use common denominators, and convert division to multiplication by a reciprocal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Substitute signed mixed numbers into eight expressions, including products and grouped fraction numerators.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine powers of negative numbers with signed arithmetic, including fractional bases.

questions.methodNote: Evaluate powers before multiplication and signed addition/subtraction, following Examples 15–16. Extend signed multiplication to fractional bases and use common denominators as in Examples 18 and 20.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine powers of negative numbers with signed arithmetic, including fractional bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Divide by signed fractions and distinguish division by a negative fraction from division by its square.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–c directly apply reciprocal multiplication to positive and negative divisors. Part d combines that method with evaluating the squared negative fraction first, so order of operations with indices is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 21 Example 20 changes division by a fraction into multiplication by its reciprocal and applies signed arithmetic. Pages 14–15 establish that a bracketed negative base is squared as a whole and powers are evaluated before division. Page 12 supplies the quotient sign rules.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Divide by signed fractions and distinguish division by a negative fraction from division by its square.

classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate three adjoining pair sums to determine and check three unknown integers in each puzzle.

questions.mappingNote: The triangle puzzles extend signed addition and subtraction through coordinated numerical reasoning; the solutions use numerical comparisons and checks rather than simultaneous algebraic equations.
questions.methodNote: Page 7 explains addition of negative integers as subtraction of their opposites. Page 8 explains subtraction of negative integers as addition of their opposites. Use these signed-arithmetic rules to find circle values and verify every adjoining pair sum.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Coordinate three adjoining pair sums to determine and check three unknown integers in each puzzle.

classification.difficultyReason: Arrange three signed integers to produce each specified sum and difference.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Arrange three signed integers to produce each specified sum and difference.

questions.methodNote: Adding a negative integer subtracts its opposite; subtracting a negative integer adds its opposite. Evaluate the resulting additions and subtractions in order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Arrange three signed integers to obtain each specified sum-and-difference target.

questions.methodNote: Page 8 teaches that subtracting a negative number adds its opposite, and demonstrates evaluating directed-number expressions with aligned working.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a missing negative integer in a number sentence involving subtraction and addition.

questions.methodNote: Page 14 contrasts an expression with and without brackets. Page 15 states that brackets are evaluated first, followed by multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction; Examples 15 and 16 demonstrate successive evaluation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select brackets, including nested brackets, to obtain specified integer results.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare sequential evaluation with pairing, then extend the pair pattern to a hundred-term sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Reverse the mean calculation to recover the original and remaining totals, account for the reduced count, and subtract the totals to identify the deleted number.

questions.methodNote: Review question 17 defines the average as the sum divided by the number of numbers and demonstrates this using both division and fraction notation. Reverse that relationship to recover each total.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recover two totals from their averages and compare them to find the deleted value.

questions.methodNote: Page 7 interprets adding negative integers and equates addition of a negative with subtraction. Page 8 demonstrates separate aligned calculation steps. Question 7 on page 27 explicitly supplies pairing consecutive terms as a method for an alternating sum; Question 10a supplies the corresponding pairs of even numbers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise equal negative differences and use repeated pairs to evaluate a long alternating sum.

classification.difficultyReason: Select opposite-sign factors giving the least product, using integer multiplication and ordering.

questions.methodNote: Page 2 establishes integer ordering on the number line. Page 11 teaches that opposite-sign factors give a negative product and two negative factors give a positive product. Example 12 on page 12 demonstrates evaluating signed products.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select opposite-sign factors giving the least product, using integer multiplication and ordering.

questions.methodNote: Page 20, Example 18, demonstrates adding and subtracting signed fractions by converting to a common denominator and simplifying. Page 21 confirms that ordinary positive-fraction methods extend to negative fractions. Evaluate the denominator products before combining the signed fractions.
